newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet to offer passengers promotional fares.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet to offer passengers promotional fares.

text.p: ValuJet President Lewis Jordan said on Friday the airline would offer special lower fares to win back passengers after federal authorities give its planes permission to fly again.

"I think in the first few days we want to have some fun with some introductory fares," he told CNN. He estimated it could be two or three weeks, or longer if aviation agency officials have more questions, before the airline could resume service.

Jordan said in television interviews the airline would continue to be a low-priced carrier and would offer the same "affordable" fares despite the cost of compliance with Federal Aviation Administration requirements imposed to permit it to resume operations.
The company cannot advertise or take reservations until it has final approval from the Department of Transportation.

As a result of the government's extensive review, Jordan said the airline would rely on only two outside contractors for heavy maintenance and had revised its training programmes and maintenance manuals and hired a senior vice president for maintenance.

"We conserved cash during this difficult period of time so we come back very strong," he told ABC's Good Morning America. He said the Department of Transportation reviewed the airline's balance sheet and determined it was financially strong enough to return to service.

"We have a lot of money in the bank," he said. "We will pass along the same affordable fares that the public wants. We have over $200 million in cash. Even if we spend $50 million on the shutdown, that leaves us with a lot of cash."
Atlanta-based ValuJet was grounded on June 17 after a heightened safety inspection of the carrier following a crash in the Florida Everglades on May 11 that killed 110 people.
The FAA said on Thursday it had returned the carrier's operating certificate after a review found it had corrected maintenance and operation failings that led to the grounding.

After a period for government review of any response to the proposed approval, the airline could fly nine planes at first and up to 15 over the next several days. Before it was grounded, ValuJet flew 51 aircraft.

The shutdown and the cost of changes instituted at the airline will be a one-time charge against expenses, Jordan said. In response to concerns the company could not make a profit while following stricter safety rules and holding down fares, he said: "We cut out hot meals and frequent flyer programmes. We don't do company cars and we don't do fancy furniture, but we spend all the money necessary for top-notch maintenance programmes and that is exactly what the FAA has just found."
